claims.text: Reversible formation and dissolution of short-range-order domains occurs at high temperatures in refractory BCC high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW.
Dynamic SRO evolution modulates dislocation mobility in refractory BCC high-entropy alloys.
Dynamic SRO evolution modulates local elastic heterogeneity.
SRO evolution governs increased yield strength during high-temperature mechanical loading.
SRO evolution governs anomalous nonlinear thermoelastic behavior during loading and unloading.
The proposed as-cast or homogenized initial state lacks pronounced preexisting SRO.
Rapid quenching will freeze in a higher SRO level than slow cooling.
Slow cooling will produce equilibrium chemical disorder.
Formation and dissolution of SRO domains alter the local elastic landscape.
SRO-induced changes in the local elastic landscape increase resistance to dislocation motion.
Higher retained SRO in quenched samples produces enhanced local lattice distortions.
The enhanced local distortions associated with SRO act as dynamic obstacles to dislocation motion.
Quenched high-SRO samples will have higher yield strength than slow-cooled samples.
Quenched high-SRO samples will show a more pronounced nonlinear thermoelastic recovery than slow-cooled samples.
Quenched samples will exhibit larger loading- and unloading-induced lattice-parameter shifts than slow-cooled samples.
Slow-cooled baseline samples exhibit a predictable linear thermoelastic response.
Slow-cooled baseline samples have lower yield strength than quenched samples.
The proposed SRO mechanism applies to refractory BCC high-entropy alloys between 800°C and 1200°C in inert atmospheres.
The central role of SRO in the proposed mechanical and thermoelastic behavior is supported by metallurgical theory and indirect evidence.
